description: Take the Great Mosque of Djenne apart piece by piece in 3D, and read the story of the largest mud-brick building on Earth, replastered by its whole town every single year.

intro: It is the largest mud building on Earth, and every spring the entire town climbs its walls to give it a new skin of plaster. This is the mosque that is rebuilt once a year.
page_title: Great Mosque of Djenne: Exploded 3D Model and History | Architectural Atlas

sections.body: A mosque has stood on this ground since the 13th century, when Djenne flourished as a trading city between the Niger and Bani rivers. The current building was raised in 1906 and 1907, when the French administration had the ruined old mosque rebuilt under Ismaila Traore, the head of Djenne's guild of masons. It is the masterpiece of Sudano-Sahelian architecture: sun-baked mud bricks called ferey, mud mortar, and a smooth coat of mud plaster over walls several feet thick, on a 75-meter platform raised 3 meters against the floods.
sections.heading: The mosque of mud

sections.body: The east wall, the qibla facing Mecca, is dominated by three great box-like minarets, the central about 16 meters tall. Each is crowned with a cone-shaped spire topped by an ostrich egg. Pilaster buttresses ring the walls, and from every face protrude bundles of rodier palm sticks called toron. They look like decoration. They are scaffolding: the building was designed with its own maintenance system built into the walls, because the mud must be renewed every year or the rains will dissolve it.
sections.heading: Towers, eggs and scaffolding

sections.body: Inside, the prayer hall measures 26 by 50 meters and is carried by nine interior walls pierced with pointed arches, creating a forest of 90 massive pillars that keeps the hall cool even in the Saharan heat. Small vents in the roof let hot air rise out. Beside the hall lies a courtyard with galleries on three sides. The whole building breathes: banco plaster of mud, grain husks, shea butter and baobab powder, shaped by hand, softened by decades of replastering into organic curves.
sections.heading: The cool forest inside

sections.body: Every spring, Djenne holds the Crepissage, the plastering festival. The plaster is mixed in pits for days, stirred by children playing in it, then carried up the toron scaffolding by the town's masons while music plays and food is shared. Without this day, the mosque would melt back into the earth within a few rainy seasons. In 1988 UNESCO listed the Old Towns of Djenne as a World Heritage Site, and the Aga Khan Trust for Culture restored the mosque from 2010 to 2012. But the real conservation is the festival: the building survives because the town refuses to let it go.
sections.heading: The festival that keeps it standing

sections.body:
The mosque has never needed a starring film role; it is the establishing shot of an entire architectural tradition. Since its UNESCO listing in 1988 it has become the single most reproduced image of Sudano-Sahelian building, the cover photograph of books on African architecture and the obligatory stop on every documentary about Mali.

Its most reported cultural moment comes every spring, when the international press covers the Crepissage. The image of the whole town plastering the mosque, broadcast from the BBC to National Geographic, turned a maintenance ritual into one of the world's most famous festivals of architecture, and made the toron beams the most recognizable scaffolding on Earth.

The building also carries a political afterlife. As the largest adobe structure in the world, it is routinely invoked in debates about sustainable building: a monumental architecture made of mud, straw and shea butter, cooled without machines, maintained by its community for a century. In that conversation the mosque is not a relic but a working argument.
sections.heading: In the cultural conversation

timeline.text: The first mosque is built on the site as Djenne flourishes on the trans-Saharan trade.
The French administration has the ruined mosque rebuilt under master mason Ismaila Traore.
The Old Towns of Djenne are listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The Aga Khan Trust for Culture restores the mosque.
The Crepissage: the whole town replasters the mosque in a one-day festival.
